chapter_theme: Payapati reaches the Jina shrine with flower and water offerings; the Lord appears under an asoka tree with throne, halo, umbrella, whisks, flower rain and heavenly music, and the king bows and sings a hymn praising his feet, his freedom from deeds and his rule above Indra and the dark-blue god.

cast.role: King Payapati, who comes to the Jina shrine and sings his hymn
the Lord or Jina, the knower, who appears under the asoka tree
the singers, dancers and praisers who crowd the shrine
the yakshas who hold the whisks beside the Lord
the gods who worship from the sky
the Vidyadharas who gather in the air with the kinnara pairs
the gem-hued red-eyed lord, with the golden-discus lord, who come beside the Lord
the queens who accompany the two lords

1886.reading: Flower offerings fall in rows like a rain, bee-loud clusters of blossom pour down, auspicious banners spread, and the hosts of binding deeds are said to have hidden away.
1886.nuance: The last line is reported speech (என்பவே), so the vanishing of karma is the poet's report of the scene, not an event he claims to see; the verse does not say whose presence drives the karma away.
1886.event: Flowers rain and banners spread as the hosts of karma are said to hide.

1887.reading: Singers, those who wish long life, dancers and those who praise the knower gather in crowds until no open space is left anywhere.

1888.reading: The poet asks us to hear how the oil-bright spearman fares as the seven-fold festival goes to the feet of the one who cast out the foes that are his deeds and taught the scripture's way aright.
1888.nuance: The verse turns the story from the hall to the shrine and names the Lord only by what he did; the festival's seven parts are not listed.

claims.claim: the Jina cast out the enemy deeds and taught the path of the scripture rightly

1889.reading: Arranging offerings of water, perfume and bee-loud flowers, the king, among the roar of his army, reaches the fair Jina shrine of the meritorious one.
1889.nuance: The king is not named in the verse; he is known from the sarukkam's earlier verses.
1889.event: Payapati arrives at the Jina shrine with water, perfume and flower offerings.

1890.reading: At the gate of the high-towered shrine the king halts his young elephant, climbs down, takes bright flowers and circles the rich city with its gardens before arriving.
1890.event: Payapati dismounts at the shrine gate and circles it with flowers in his hand.

1891.reading: As the king arrives, the Lord appears seated on a lion throne beneath an asoka tree in the gold-adorned city, shining together with its light.
1891.nuance: The asoka and the throne begin a series of the Jina's signs, the shade tree, flowers, music, whisks, throne, halo and umbrella, that the next verses spread across the scene.
1891.event: The Lord appears to Payapati on a lion throne under an asoka tree.

1892.reading: The throne is said to be gold set with rows of red gems, carved with elephant-trunk lions and sea-monster mouths, and its look spills five kinds of light.
1892.nuance: Only the throne is described; the Lord seated on it is not.

1893.reading: When the world sees the thousand-ray light, the darkness of the seven worlds leaves and deeds are said to wither; a ring of light appears around the Lord.
1893.nuance: The second line is hard (ஆழியல் வினை கேளாடவிய), so whether the deeds wither or the dark withdraws from them is a reading; the halo (பாமண்டலம்) is not named.

claims.claim: the Jina's halo clears the darkness of the worlds and dries up the deeds of those who see it

1894.reading: Yakshas with shoulders like tall trees raise whisks that look like milk-white moonbeams settled on masses of gem, their hands joined in worship.
1894.nuance: The whisks stand among the eight signs of the Jina, borne by divine servants, not by the king's own men.

1895.reading: The umbrella of the fragrant-tree Lord is a cluster of three, drinkable-bright with moonlike pearls, hemmed with gold and rich with light.
1895.nuance: The three umbrellas answer the single white umbrella of the earthly king, who elsewhere rules the world under one; here a triple one rises over the Jina.

1896.reading: Flaming flowers on the asoka that seem to feed a fire, ponds of lotus, and swarms of bees on the leafy asoka cool the place.
1896.nuance: The asoka's red blooms look like fire but cool, so the image of heat is turned to calm.

1897.reading: Banners like the sides of cloud-eyed women spread in rows, shapes like rain of song appear, and a rain of flowers buries the golden ground.
1897.nuance: The flower rain here is the divine counterpart of the offered flowers in 1886.

1898.reading: Gods clap their hands in worship, and sweet music sounds sadly on every side beneath rain-heavy flowers that mingle in the dark sky.
1898.nuance: இரங்கி suggests the music sounds yearning, as if grieved; the verse does not say for what.

1899.reading: Vidyadhara men and women with dark-eyed, wide-hipped companions mingle with pairs of kinnaras rising all over the upper air.
1899.nuance: Each class of heavenly being is named by line, without any word on what the Lord does for them.

1900.reading: The red-eyed gem-coloured one of the flame-bright crown, the one of the golden discus, and their queens appear beside the Lord of the rare gem hue.
1900.nuance: The two gem-coloured figures are not named; the red eyes point to Tivittan of the earlier sarukkam and the golden discus to a discus-holder, but the verse does not fix who they are.
1900.event: Two gem-hued lords and their queens come to stand beside the Lord.

1901.reading: Seeing the gem-and-gold city that heaven's builders made, a sight to take away the eye, the king, whose deeds were shaking loose, stood as sovereign.
1901.nuance: விண்டுதிர் வினையினன் vaguely says the king's deeds are dropping away; the verse leaves open whether that is cause or result of what he sees. The last words (வேந்தனாயினான்) are unusual, since he was already king.
1901.event: Payapati sees the divine city and stands before the Lord.

1902.reading: Having anointed the ground with perfume and set many flowers as ornaments, the king bows until his gem-crown touches the earth and, his deeds already cut, begins his hymn to the Lord.
1902.nuance: துணிபடு வினையினன் is said of the worshipper before the hymn begins, so the cutting of deeds comes with the act of devotion, not after the praise.
1902.event: Payapati prepares the ground, bows with his crown to the earth and begins to praise the Lord.

claims.claim: worship at the Jina's feet is bowing that cuts the deeds

1903.reading: The king asks of the Lord, whose white umbrella's shade and gem-bright light put the sun and moon to shame, whether his red feet were reddened by the lotus-petals touching them or whether their red rays took the shape of flowers.
1903.nuance: The poet turns the Lord's feet into a question about cause (do the lotuses redden them, or the feet the lotuses?), a conceit of praise, not a doctrine; the stanza is printed in eight half-lines and was joined into four.
1903.event: Payapati's hymn begins with a question about the Lord's red feet.

1904.reading: The king says the Lord cut the dark garlands of fierce deeds, spread the bright light of unending knowledge and gave a fair path; his servants know only to praise his feet, but those who do not know his greatness and quarrel can have the quarrel of deeds removed.
1904.nuance: The last line (பிணங்குவார் தம்மை வினைப் பிணக்கொழிக்கலாமே) is hard: it may say the disputants' own deeds are ended by worship, or the Lord's power could end the quarrel of deeds in them. Also read the half-line division: the stanza is printed in eight half-lines and was joined into four.

claims.claim: the Jina destroyed his deeds, spread unending knowledge and taught a good path
those who dispute the Lord's greatness are bound by a quarrel of deeds that can be undone

1905.reading: Shall I say you spread as light and as the world, or that the world lies within your light, that you rule the world with grace, that heaven has taken your feet; shall I say you spread true being, or that true being spread as you spread it? Only by understanding your feet will it be known.
1905.nuance: The repeated என்கோ (shall I say) lets the hymn put two ways of speaking side by side, the Lord as source and the Lord as container, without choosing; the king says the choice is settled only by understanding.

claims.claim: the Jina's light is the world and the world is contained in his light
the real can be known only by understanding the Lord's feet

1906.reading: The Lord is the one who gives light to the thousand-eyed Indra, who is the beginning of ages, spreads to the world's measure, harms no living thing, is easy for those who worship his feet; how then can anyone count any other as god?
1906.nuance: Indra, the four-tusked elephant's owner of thousand eyes (line 1), is placed beneath the Jina as a receiver of his light, which turns the heaven's lord into a worshipper. The rival god is not named; the claim is aimed at any other claimant.

claims.claim: no one but the Jina may be reckoned the Lord
the Lord harms no living being and is easy for his worshippers

1907.reading: The king asks why, when the golden feet are held by celestials with unblinking eyes, the dark gods' world is flooded by his light, and the discus-lord with his hand on his crown stands to one side, the wheel of grace goes in front and others follow; is there a heaven that does not lie at his feet?
1907.nuance: The question pattern (தெருளாமையால் வினவற்பாலது) is a deferential form: the poet claims not to know why, though the question itself carries the claim. The discus-lord is not named and may be Vishnu or a world-emperor.

claims.claim: every heaven lies at the Jina's feet and the wheel of grace goes before the rest

1908.reading: The king says that the Lord's feet are above even the talk about the garlanded crown of the dark-blue lord whom the heavens praise, and that if the feet do not touch the lotus offered by those who go to carry it, it means that the lack of those who would stand at his feet has been known.
1908.nuance: Lines 3 and 4 are very hard and turn on the sense of அடியுறுவார் இன்மை; the reading here is cautious. If the dark-blue lord is Vishnu, the verse shows a Jain poet placing Vishnu at the Jina's feet, a claim the poet voices, not a view of Vaishnavas.

claims.claim: the Lord surpasses the dark-blue discus-bearing god, who bows to him

links.note: 1886 has offered flowers falling in a rain at the king's approach; 1897 has a divine rain of flowers burying the golden ground at the Lord's appearance.
links.teaches: The same flower rain is first the king's offering and then the heavens' answer, so the worship and its reception share one image.

links.note: 1902 has the crowned king bow until the gem-crown touches the earth; Kural 9 says a head that does not bow at the feet of the eight-quality one is a useless organ.
links.teaches: The couplet's useless head becomes the crowned one of a king who sets power on the ground, which shows what the bow costs a ruler.

gains.a: The king's bow gains a stated reason, that a head which will not bow is as dead as a sense that does not sense.
gains.b: The couplet gains a ruler whose head carries a crown, so the bow costs a pride the couplet's speaker does not mention.

links.note: 1903 asks whether the Lord's red feet are reddened by lotus petals or by their own rays; 181 has the king praising the red lotus feet of him who conquered the dust of deeds.
links.teaches: The red feet appear in both shrine hymns, first as a fact and then as a riddle of cause, so the later hymn plays on the earlier plain praise.

links.note: 1904 says the Lord cut off the dark garlands of fierce deeds; Kural 5 says the two deeds born of darkness do not cling to those devoted to the Lord's true praise.
links.teaches: The Lord is shown in 1904 as the one who has already done what the couplet promises his devotees, so the cause of their freedom is his own freeing.

gains.a: The hymn gains a stated result for the praiser, that the two kinds of deeds will not cling to him.
gains.b: The couplet gains a named doer who has cut his own deeds, which it leaves unsaid.

links.note: 1904 says those who do not grasp the Lord's greatness quarrel and are bound by a quarrel of deeds; 182 says that even when called the knower of all the Lord is hard to truly know.
links.teaches: The earlier verse says why the Lord is hard to know and the later says what follows from not knowing him, which is the quarrel that binds.

links.note: 1906 says there is no other god to count, and the Lord is easy for those who worship his feet; Kural 7 says only those who reach the feet of the one without a peer can remove the mind's anxiety.
links.teaches: The hymn names its peerless one by what he does to living things, while the couplet leaves the feet unnamed and so open to any tradition.

gains.a: The hymn gains the couplet's claim that the anxieties of the mind are removed only by those feet.
gains.b: The couplet gains a candidate for the one without a peer, whose peerlessness is given as harmlessness and ease of access.

links.note: 1906 says no one but the Lord, who harms no life, can be counted as god; Tirumanthiram 1451 says there is one God in all ten directions and bids us take refuge in his feet to dry up the sea of deeds.
links.teaches: Both hold one God whose feet end the deeds, but they name different ones, and the pair turns on whether the one at whose feet deeds are shed is a Jina who gave up his own, or a God who gives grace.

gains.a: The hymn gains a rival that makes the same demand, to take refuge at one pair of feet, but on the strength of a different god.
gains.b: The verse gains a Jain claim that the Lord who deserves such refuge is the Jina, who has no part in creating or ruling.

source_issues: Verses 1903 to 1908 are printed in eight half-lines in the source and were joined into four lines each by the build; the joins follow the metre.
Lines 3 and 4 of 1908 and line 4 of 1904 are hard to parse; the readings given are marked uncertain.
